Learning Objectives
Describe the most common etiologies of hip pain based on the location of pain.
Understand the key components of a complete physical examination of the hip.
Recognize important components of the patient history to aid in narrowing the differential
diagnosis.

Hip pain is common but often complex. Hip pain may be perceived from the hip joint,
from surrounding soft tissues, and from other organ systems. Therefore, a thorough
patient history and physical examination are essential to correctly determine the
diagnosis. A thorough physical examination of the hip requires observation, palpation of
the surrounding soft tissues, gait analysis, range of motion (ROM) assessment, and other
provocative maneuvers. The authors of this lesson recommend creating a standard hip
examination for all patients so that essential aspects of the physical examination are
never missed or forgotten. Key components of the patient history are then used to fine
tune the physical examination so that provocative maneuvers are performed on a case-
by-case basis. Surgeons should understand the most common etiologies of hip pain and
how to perform a thorough patient history and physical examination of the hip joint
(Resource 1).
Etiologies of Hip Pain
Overview of hip pain
Causes and symptoms commonly associated with hip pain
Hip pain is common, and it may be episodic or chronic. It often is localized to three main
areas: the anterior hip and groin area, the posterior hip and buttock, or the lateral hip.
Hip pain may be related to intra-articular or extra-articular pathology.
Referred pain to the thigh or knee also may occur, particularly in patients with hip arthritis.
Common etiologies of hip pain based on presenting location
Anterior pain (front of leg)
Anterior hip/groin pain suggests pain within the hip joint itself.
Possible diagnoses include arthritis (inflammatory and osteoarthritis), femoroacetabular
impingement, developmental dysplasia of the hip, iliopsoas tendinitis, fracture (including
stress fractures), transient synovitis, transient osteoporosis, athletic pubalgia, septic
arthritis, labral tear, and osteonecrosis.
Lateral pain (side of leg)
The most common diagnosis for lateral pain is greater trochanteric bursitis.
The differential diagnosis for lateral hip pain includes greater trochanteric bursitis,
iliotibial band (ITB) syndrome, abductor tendinitis, abductor tendon tear, and snapping of
the ITB over the trochanter.
Posterior pain (back of leg)

The most common cause of posterior hip pain is lumbar radiculopathy.
Posterior pain suggests radiculopathy, sacroiliitis hamstring tendinitis, and piriformis
syndrome (Video 1).
Video 1 Weber K: Special tests: Piriformis test, from Physical examination of the hip and thigh,
in Armstrong AD, Hubbard MC, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 5. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 566-573.

Etiologies of Hip Pain
Hip pain is common in patients of all ages. Although most hip pathology can be
managed nonsurgically, a correct diagnosis is essential in guiding treatment decisions.
Patients may perceive hip pain in multiple locations, including the groin, lateral hip,
buttock area, proximal thigh, or lower back. In addition, patients with hip arthritis also
may experience pain radiating to the thigh and knee. Some patients with certain hip
injuries, such as arthritis, feel pain only in the knee; this is called referred pain.
Knowledge of the most common etiologies of hip pain, depending on the location of
perceived pain, allows clinicians to narrow the differential diagnosis to focus the
physical examination and imaging studies.

One of the challenges in accurately diagnosing hip pain is that overlap often occurs
between hip joint pathology and lumbosacral spine pathology. The physical
examination helps elucidate if pain is related to the hip or the spine; however,
occasionally, a diagnostic injection or additional imaging studies may be necessary.
Patient History
Important factors used to narrow the differential diagnosis include the age of the patient, the
location of the pain, and whether the pain was caused by a traumatic event.
A description of the pain also is helpful, including when the pain occurs (eg, in the morning, at
night), the length of time the pain has been present, the character of the pain (eg, sharp, dull),
whether the pain is episodic or constant, the mechanism of any injury, activities that worsen
the pain, and interventions that alleviate the pain.

Patient History
Although the differential diagnosis for hip pain may be extensive, three components of
the patient history allow the clinician to narrow the focus during the physical
examination: the age of the patient, the location of the pain, and whether the pain
occurred after a traumatic event.
Other aspects of the patient history that should be elicited from all patients include the
length of time the pain has been present, when the pain occurs (ie, the time of day or
night), the mechanism of any injury, the character of the pain (dull, sharp, achy),
activities that worsen the pain (ie, weight-bearing activities, sleeping on the hip), and
interventions the patient has attempted to relieve the pain. In particular, clinicians must
determine if the patient has attempted rest, ice, heat, NSAIDs, physical therapy,
exercises, orthoses/braces, activity modifications, use of an assistive device (eg, cane,
crutches), injections (eg, corticosteroids), or surgical treatment. If clinical concern for
osteonecrosis exists, then questions should be asked about alcohol use, tobacco use,
and steroid use and the patient’s history of clotting disorders.

Hip pain often is confused with lumbar spine/radicular pain. Common clues taken from
the patient history that indicate a patient has radicular symptoms include describing the
pain as burning or shooting or pain radiating below the knee and associated with
numbness or weakness in the foot or toes (eg, extensor hallucis longus). Because the
femur ends at the knee, pain felt below the knee often is not caused by hip pathology.
Red flags in the patient history include pain at night, associated fevers, or pain with
passive movement. In patients who report these symptoms, malignancy and/or infection
should be ruled out or considered during the workup.
Physical Examination
Clinicians should develop a consistent and efficient hip physical examination that includes
assessment of the patient’s gait and the strength of the surrounding hip musculature,
palpation of the surrounding soft tissues, and ROM assessment (Resource 2).
Provocative tests can then be performed, depending on the patient’s description of the
location of the pain, the presence of a traumatic event, and the age of the patient. The tests
are tailored to the most common etiologies included the clinician’s differential diagnosis.

Physical Examination
Several studies have published detailed physical examinations that evaluate the hip in a
multilayered fashion, including the osteochondral, capsulolabral, musculotendinous,
neurovascular, and kinetic chain sections of the physical examination.1 Although this
published material is an excellent resource for a detailed and comprehensive physical
examination, residents and clinicians should develop their own focused and complete
physical examination (Resource 3).
Before the physician examines the hip, the patient should be asked to point to the
location of the pain with one finger to further focus the physical examination and narrow
the differential diagnosis. Occasionally, patients demonstrate the C sign, in which the
patient holds the hand in a C shape, and places it in the abductor region above the
greater trochanter, with the thumb in the buttock region and the fingers in the groin.

The C sign often is mistakenly assumed to indicate that the patient is pointing to the
lateral soft tissues; however, this sign often indicates intra-articular pathology.2 The
contralateral hip always is examined first to attain an assessment of normal for that
particular patient, so it can be compared with the painful hip.
Standing Portion of the Physical Examination
Key aspects of the standing portion of the hip physical examination include observation of the
manner in which a patient rises from a seated position, evaluation of the patient’s stance, and
gait analysis.
The clinician should note whether the shoulders and pelvis are level with the patient standing.
A Trendelenburg gait may indicate abductor weakness.
An antalgic or coxalgic gait is characterized by a decreased stance phase secondary to pain.
An in-toeing gait may indicate increased femoral anteversion, whereas out-toeing may indicate
decreased femoral anteversion.

Standing Portion of the Physical Examination
The first step in the physical examination is to have the patient stand up from the
examination table or chair. A number of observations can be made from simply having
the patient stand, including how difficult it is for the patient to rise, a facial expression
made because of pain, and whether the hip joint can be fully extended. After the patient
is standing, the clinician should observe whether the shoulders are level and determine
whether pelvic obliquity is present. These may signify that the patient has a functional or
true leg-length discrepancy (LLD). Common causes of pelvic obliquity include scoliosis,
hip flexion contracture, or true LLD. In patients with hip arthritis who have true LLD,
blocks can be placed under the affected foot to estimate the degree of LLD (Video 2).

Video 2 Weber K: Inspection/palpation: Posterior view, from Physical examination of the
hip and thigh, in Armstrong AD, Hubbard MC, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 5.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 566-573.
Next, the patient’s gait is assessed (Video 3). Abnormal gait patterns may be related to
compensation because of pain or muscular weakness around the hip joint. Gait should
be assessed in the hallway (provided the patient agrees) so that the full stride can be
assessed. Components that should be assessed include the foot progression angle,
pelvic position, length of time in stance phase, and stride length.3 An abnormal foot
progression angle may be related to static malalignment observed with abnormal
femoral version. A patient with in-toeing may have increased femoral anteversion,
whereas a patient with out-toeing may have reduced femoral anteversion. A
Trendelenburg gait may be observed in patients with abductor weakness. In a
Trendelenburg gait pattern, patients raise the pelvis on the affected side and drop the
contralateral pelvis because they adduct the leg (Video 4). Conversely, patients with an
antalgic or coxalgic gait related to pain demonstrate a shortened stance phase on the
affected side. In assessment of the patient’s stride length, posterior pain that is felt
during hip extension may suggest ischiofemoral impingement,4 whereas posterior pain
with hip flexion may indicate hamstring pathology5 (Resources 4 and 5).

Supine Portion of Hip Physical Examination
A comprehensive supine physical examination of the hip should include a leg length
assessment; inspection of the skin and previous incisions; passive ROM assessment, including
evaluation for the presence of a hip flexion contracture; the flexion, abduction, external
rotation test; the flexion, adduction, internal rotation (FADDIR) test; the Stinchfield test; and
palpation of the soft tissues around the hip joint.
The contralateral limb should be assessed before examining the painful hip.
Palpation of the surrounding soft tissues should be performed based on the location at which
the patient feels pain.
Lateral pain with palpation may be related to trochanteric bursitis or ITB syndrome (Video 5).
Ischial tuberosity pain may be related to hamstring injury or sciatic nerve neuropathy or
neuritis.
The Thomas test is used to assess for a hip flexion contracture (Video 6).
The test is begun with both knees flexed to the chest.
The patient then holds the contralateral, unaffected knee in place while extending the
affected, painful leg.
Inability to extend the hip flat indicates a hip flexion contracture.
The flexion, abduction, external rotation test can distinguish between sacroiliac joint pain and
hip pain.
The FADDIR test often is positive in patients with femoroacetabular impingement or a labral
tear.
A positive Stinchfield test indicates an intra-articular source of hip pain, including iliopsoas
tendinitis (Figure 1).
Pain with active hip flexion may be caused by iliopsoas tendinitis.
Additional tests that can be performed to assess for impingement in select patients include
the Dynamic Internal Rotatory Impingement test, and the Dynamic External Rotatory
Impingement test.

Figure 1 Clinical photograph shows the Stinchfield test, which is performed with the patient in
the supine position. The examiner applies downward pressure as the patient actively elevates the
leg to 30°. (Reproduced from Suarez JC, Ely EE, Mutnal AB, et al: Comprehensive approach to the
evaluation of groin pain. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2013;21[9]:558-70.)

Supine Portion of Hip Physical Examination
Some patients are wheelchair bound and cannot be examined in the supine position.
However, the authors of this lesson believe that most patients should be examined in
the supine position. The contralateral (unaffected) hip should be examined first. Before
examining the patient, the clinician should observe how easily the patient is able to lift
the leg onto the examination table. Difficulty lifting the leg on to the examination table
may be a sign of intra-articular pathology (such as arthritis) or iliopsoas tendinitis. With
the patient lying flat on the examination table, the surgeon can further assess if the
patient has an LLD by observing the position of the medial malleolus on both ankles.
Palpation of the soft tissues about the hip joint should be focused, based on the location
the patient describes the pain. Pain felt with palpation over the ischial tuberosity
suggests hamstring tendinitis or sciatic neuropathy/neuritis if the pain is burning or
shooting and felt down the leg. Pain with palpation laterally often is related to greater
trochanteric bursitis if located over the greater trochanter or ITB syndrome if felt down
the thigh and into the lateral aspect of the knee. Conversely, pain over the anterior
superior iliac spine may be related to sartorius avulsion or injury.

Passive hip flexion is then assessed. In assessing passive hip flexion, the pelvic position
should be noted after terminal flexion is reached. In patients with a severely arthritic hip
joint, the pelvis may rise off of the examination table at terminal hip flexion, giving a
false impression of continued hip flexion. Similarly, to determine if a patient has a hip
flexion contracture, the examiner should ask the patient to hold both knees to the chest
to establish a neutral pelvic inclination and then hold the contralateral, unaffected knee
in place while extending the affected, painful hip (Thomas test). If the patient is unable to
bring the leg flat on the examination table, the patient likely has a flexion contracture. In
general, the clinician should obtain passive measurements of hip flexion (normal is 125°
to 135°), extension (normal is 20° to 30°), external rotation (normal is approximately 40°
to 50°), internal rotation (normal is approximately 20° to 30°), abduction (normal is 40°
to 50°), and adduction (normal is 20° to 30°). Although normal values are listed, they are
estimates, and ROM measurements should always be compared with those of the
contralateral limb to assess the restriction in ROM in each individual patient (Video 7).
Active hip flexion also can be assessed in certain patients. Pain with active hip flexion
often is a sign of iliopsoas tendinitis. Similarly, pain experienced during active extension
of the hip from a flexed position while lying supine also may indicate iliopsoas tendinitis
(Videos 8 and 9).

thigh, in Armstrong AD, Hubbard MC, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 5.

The flexion, abduction, external rotation test may be useful in distinguishing intra-
articular hip pain from extra-articular pain and in differentiating pain related to the hip
from that related to the sacroiliac joint. In this maneuver, the clinician brings the affected
hip into hip flexion and abducts and externally rotates the hip to the maximum limits of
motion (depending on the pain). Pain that is reproduced (ie, the same pain the patient
presented with) may be a sign of posterolateral acetabular incongruence/injury or
musculotendinous abductor or iliopsoas injury; however, pain that is felt more
posteriorly near the sacroiliac joint usually confirms that the etiology is sacroiliac joint
pain rather than pain from the hip joint itself.
In the FADDIR test, the clinician flexes, adducts, and internally rotates the affected hip
joint. This test is most commonly performed in patients in whom impingement and/or a
labral tear is suspected because patients with hip arthritis often cannot tolerate this
examination maneuver. Pain with the FADDIR test confirms that the pain is intra-
articular in the hip joint (Video 10).
The clinician can perform the Stinchfield test if it remains unclear whether the pain is
intra-articular. In this test, the clinician places the patient in the supine position with the
knee extended and asks the patient to resist hip flexion past 30° to 45° (ie, perform a
resisted straight leg raise). Pain with the Stinchfield test that is reproduced in the groin
often is a sign of intra-articular pathology, including the iliopsoas.

Prone Physical Examination
For the femoral anteversion test, the patient is placed in the prone position, with the knees
flexed to 90°.
The clinician rotates the leg through the knee, and femoral anteversion is assessed by noting
the angle formed between the axis of the tibia and an imaginary vertical line.
Normal femoral anteversion is between 10° and 20°.

Prone Physical Examination
Most of the hip physical examination is performed in the supine position; however, the
femoral anteversion test can be performed in the prone position. Femoral anteversion
may be assessed in patients who have an abnormal foot progression angle or abnormal
ROM, even on the unaffected side. With the femoral anteversion test, the patient is
placed in the prone position, with the knees flexed to 90°. The clinician rotates the leg
through the knee, and femoral anteversion is assessed by noting the angle formed
between the axis of the tibia and an imaginary vertical line. In assessing femoral
anteversion, the greater trochanter should be palpated and confirmed to be in the most
lateral position possible. Normal femoral anteversion is between 10° and 20°.
Lateral Physical Examination
The Ober test is used to assess the tightness of the ITB.

Lateral Physical Examination

Select patients in whom suspicion exists that the pain may be attributed to the ITB can
be examined in the lateral position. The most common test performed in the lateral
position is the Ober test. In this test, the patient is placed in the lateral decubitus
position with the affected hip toward the ceiling; the affected leg is abducted and
extended. The examiner then asks the patient to adduct the leg in the extended position.
Patients who are unable to adduct to the neutral position have a tight ITB.
Neurovascular Examination
Thorough sensory and vascular examination includes four focus areas: neurologic, radicular,
vascular, and lymphatic examinations.
For the neurologic examination, sensory nerves originating from the L2 through S1 levels and
the deep tendon reflexes of the patella (L2 through L4 spinal nerves) and the Achilles tendon
(L5 nerves) are assessed.
The straight leg raise examination can be performed to assess radicular neurologic
symptoms.
The vascular examination includes palpation of the pulses of the dorsalis pedis and posterior
tibial artery.
The lymphatic assessment focuses on skin inspection for swelling, scarring, or side-to-side
asymmetry.

Neurovascular Examination
The neurovascular and lymphatic examinations should be performed in a focused
manner. Dissimilar from spine surgery, in which a detailed neurovascular examination is
necessary to accurately diagnose the nerve or nerve root responsible for a patient’s
symptoms, in a hip physical examination, global assessment of the neurovascular
system often is acceptable.
The exception to this scenario is if the clinician suspects the hip pain is related to spinal
pathology. With the patient in the supine position, the clinician can determine if swelling
is present in the lower leg and whether the limb is asymmetric compared with the
contralateral limb. A straight leg raise test often is performed to determine or confirm

radicular symptoms. In this test, the patient is placed in the supine with the knee
extended; the examiner performs a passive straight leg raise, often with dorsiflexion of
the ankle to increase the stretch on the posterior structures. A positive straight leg test is
noted if radicular pain is felt in the posterior aspect of the limb as the affected leg or the
contralateral leg is raised. Next, with the patient in the supine position, the clinician
palpates the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial artery. If the artery cannot be palpated, a
Doppler examination can be performed.
Finally, a strength assessment of ankle dorsiflexion/plantar flexion and dorsiflexion of
the great toe should be performed on all patients. In addition, sensory examinations of
the dorsal and plantar aspects of the foot should be performed. Additional strength
assessments of the abductors, quadriceps, hamstrings, and hip flexors can be
performed depending on the main symptom and after examination of gait. Deep tendon
reflexes can be assessed in rare cases; patellar tendon reflexes assess the L2 through L4
nerve roots, whereas Achilles tendon deep tendon reflexes assess the L5-S1 nerve roots.
